title: Meta's AI buildout commitments hit $825 billion — markets flinch
subtitle: A quarterly SEC filing shows total future lease and contract obligations have climbed from roughly $700B in July to about $825B, mostly tied to compute and data centers.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Meta's quarterly SEC filing on October 22 disclosed about $825 billion in future lease and contract commitments, up from roughly $700 billion in July. The largest piece is $454.5 billion in non-cancelable contracts — cloud capacity, servers, network gear, and energy supply. A further $355.7 billion covers leases that have not yet commenced, running out as far as 30 years. Meta also raised its 2026 capital-expenditure guidance to a range of $135–145 billion.

Markets responded the same day. Meta's five-year credit default swap spread hit an intraday record, and the stock fell more than 7% in U.S. trading. The $825 billion figure is a sum of separate line items in the filing rather than a headline number Meta chose to publish, but Bloomberg's tally made the arithmetic unavoidable: at this scale, AI infrastructure financing is now a credit-market story, not just a capex story.

The numbers fit a broader pattern. Hyperscalers have been signing multi-decade power and real-estate deals to lock in future compute, which pushes obligations off the quarterly balance sheet but into the long tail of lease disclosures. For Meta specifically, this is the second large upward revision in three months, which is why debt analysts — not just equity analysts — are now in the conversation.

A note for learners: when a company's AI story moves from product pages to CDS spreads, something has shifted. Compute is capital, and capital has a cost. The useful habit is to look past the model demos to the financing structure underneath — leases, prepayments, power contracts — because that is where the real constraints on this cycle will show up first.
